title: 2026-03-20-session-heatmap-batching-prefetch-playbook-with-polaris-edge
summary: Walkthrough of Redwood Optimize recommendations for session-prefetch, prefix/KV cache policy, and batching heatmap simulation tailored to Polaris Edge's mixed short/long prompt workload. Discussed target latency SLOs, cost tradeoffs, dedicated vs hosted routing, KMS for encryption, and next steps to run a custom cost sim and pilot.
topics: sessionization and prefix cache hit patterns
cost model sensitivity to hit rate and sequence length
routing: hosted vs dedicated and fallback policies
questions: How does prefix vs full-key KV cache affect cold-starts?
What TTLs do you recommend for conversational sessions?
Can we simulate 1.5M monthly active sessions mixed 80/20 short-long?
How does dedicated capacity change unit pricing assumptions?
action_items: Maya Raghavan - run a 72-hour heatmap sim for Polaris Edge sample trace (80% short 20% long) and share CSV by 2026-03-27
Jared Kim - send tailored cost model spreadsheet with dedicated vs hosted scenarios and suggested batch sizes by 2026-03-24
Samir Patel - provide a sanitized request trace and sample session lengths (CSV) by 2026-03-23
Polaris Edge/SRE - confirm security review attendees for next call (include infosec + platform) by 2026-03-25
next_steps: Run heatmap sim and share results
Review cost model and pick pilot configuration
Schedule technical deep-dive with SRE for networking and KMS
Start a 2-week pilot on dedicated pool if numbers align
transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-03-20 16:00 UTC, duration 63m, attendees: Jared, Maya, Luis (Redwood); Eleanor, Samir, Ivy, Rajesh (Polaris Edge)

[00:00] Jared Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick check — is this time still good?
[00:06] Eleanor Wade: Yep, good here. We'll try to keep it focused, got a few execs on a tight schedule.
[00:10] Jared Kim: Great. The goal for today is to run through an Optimize playbook: prefix/K-V cache strategy, session prefetch, and then run a heatmap-style batching sim so you can see cost/latency tradeoffs with your profile. Maya will demo the console and heatmap tool, Luis will chime on kernel-level perf.
[00:28] Maya Raghavan: Hi all — quick note, I have the Polaris sample trace you sent last week loaded into the sim. I sanitized a few PII fields, okay?
[00:34] Samir Patel: Yep that's the sanitized set. We removed customer ids, kept sequence lengths and timestamps.
[00:39] Luis Ortega: Cool. Before we dive in — can you summarize your workload mix again? I want to align expectations.
[00:44] Ivy Zhou: Sure — roughly 80% of requests are short queries (1-60 tokens) — search-style prompts. The other 20% are long multimodal context expansions and chat sessions that go up to 3,000 tokens (we usually cap there).
[00:58] Maya Raghavan: Perfect. That split plays well into prefix caching: short queries often hit cached prefixes and batching helps amortize kernels. For long sessions we'll show sessionized KV caching to avoid re-computing prefix context.
[01:12] [01:12] Eleanor Wade: Our latency SLO for interactive UI is 120ms P95. For background jobs we can tolerate up to 1s.
[01:20] Jared Kim: That's helpful. We'll show a couple of simulations — one optimized for strict P95, another for cost-efficient throughput.

[05:00] Maya Raghavan: (screen share) Alright here's the heatmap UI. On the X axis is request arrival rate, Y is sequence length buckets. Colors show per-token cost and P95 latency. This first sim assumes hosted API pricing and default batch size 8 with continuous batching window 30ms. You can see in the 1-60 token bucket latencies are sub-100ms at low concurrency and cost per 1k tokens is low due to prefix hits.
[05:38] Samir Patel: I'm noticing a bright spot at medium arrival rates for the 500-1500 token bucket — what's causing that spike?
[05:44] Maya Raghavan: That's queueing — medium arrival rate means the batch window fills and we hit larger batch sizes but kernel saturation causes tail latency to jump. The sim shows tradeoff: increase concurrency (more replicas) or reduce batch window to keep latency but cost rises.
[06:02] Luis Ortega: Also worth noting some kernels scale worse with sequence length — our runtime will pick different kernels for long context which affects per-token throughput. That's why we show both cost and latency heatmaps.

[12:00] Rajesh Menon: On security — we need to ensure KV cache entries are encrypted at rest and accessible only via our KMS. How does Redwood handle that in private/dedicated?
[12:12] Jared Kim: Good question. For Private/Dedicated deployments we integrate with customer KMS (Cloud KMS/HSM). Cache artifacts are encrypted and we log key access in audit logs. For hosted we offer a managed encryption option plus an enterprise plan that can hook to your KMS via trust boundary.
[12:30] Ivy Zhou: And what about data residency? We need EU-only for a subset of traffic.
[12:35] Maya Raghavan: You can pin routing rules by region. The sim can also model mixed routing — e.g., route EU sessions to EU dedicated pool — we'll show cost delta for that.

[18:00] Maya Raghavan: Back to cache patterns. Two levers: prefix cache and session-level KV cache. Prefix cache stores decoded/encoded prefix KV states for common prompt prefixes. Session KV stores user session past KV states and is keyed by session id. In your trace I see ~30% of short queries share the same top-10 prefixes — that yields big hit rates if you precompute those KV entries.
[18:30] Eleanor Wade: How sensitive is hit rate to TTL? If we set TTL 10m vs 1h what changes?
[18:36] Maya Raghavan: TTL affects cold fraction. With your 80/20 mix, our sim shows going from 10m to 60m TTL increases prefix hit rate from 42% to 58% in this trace. But TTL also increases memory footprint on the cache nodes, so there's an infra cost. We'll include a memory/cost column in the export.

[24:00] Luis Ortega: On batching knobs: we recommend dynamic batch sizing with backpressure aware windows. For short queries, small batches (4-8) reduce latency; for long sequences, batching is less helpful because it dominates compute per-request. Consider hybrid routing: route short-only endpoints to a low-latency pool with tight batch windows; route long sessions to a throughput-optimized pool.

[28:15] Samir Patel: Can the runtime do automatic routing based on user agent or request shape? We don't want to maintain a lot of routes.
[28:22] Maya Raghavan: Yes, you can define policies in the console: predicate-based routing by average sequence length, header tags, or tenant. Policies can fall back to a cheaper model variant if capacity is constrained.

[34:00] Maya Raghavan: I'm running a quick sim: scenario A is hosted default with prefix cache on, batch window 30ms; scenario B is dedicated pool with prewarmed KV and batch window 50ms. Results here — scenario B yields 22% lower $/token at the 95th percentile throughput but P95 latency is ~15ms higher for short requests because of slightly larger aggregate batch sizes and cross-replica sync.
[34:40] Ivy Zhou: Interesting — we'd probably accept the 15ms delta if costs drop. How do we quantify the cost of reserving the dedicated pool?
[34:48] Jared Kim: The cost model spreadsheet I'll send includes amortized reserved capacity cost vs on-demand hosted. For your expected load the math tends to favor reserved when sustained utilization is above ~60% of the pool. We'll share the breakpoint for your numbers.

[40:00] Eleanor Wade: A practical concern — we have session affinity from the frontend. Does sessionized KV require sticky routing?
[40:07] Maya Raghavan: Sessionized KV benefits from affinity but we also support a distributed KV tier with consistent hashing. Sticky routing improves hit rate but adds complexity; the console shows both patterns and their hit-rate curves.

[45:30] Rajesh Menon: And failure modes — if a dedicated node goes down, how do we failover without losing KV state?
[45:37] Luis Ortega: We replicate KV entries across N replicas and maintain a write-ahead log. On failure we rebuild progressively; the system falls back to a stateless model variant temporarily which increases cost and latency but prevents data loss. We'll include RTO/RPO numbers in the SRE doc.

[50:00] Maya Raghavan: I'm exporting the sim now — sending a link to the CSV and a visual heatmap. Link: https://app.redwood.ai/sims/pe-heatmap-20260320 (note: demo link, not live share)
[50:12] Samir Patel: Great. We'll want the raw CSV to plug into our cost dashboards.

[53:00] Jared Kim: Quick note on measurement noise — transcription here may not capture every micro-interruption. But the sim includes monte-carlo runs with stochastic arrival patterns; that helps account for burstiness.

[56:00] Ivy Zhou: One more item — for regulatory reasons we need audit trails for model versioning and prompt retention. Can those be tied to cost runs?
[56:10] Maya Raghavan: Yes, Redwood Console stores per-request metadata, model version, token usage, and you can export filtered traces tied to a rollout. We can also surface eval regressions if you run canary tests.

[59:30] Eleanor Wade: OK let's recap. From Polaris side: Samir will share sanitized trace; Rajesh will confirm SRE/security folks for the next call. From Redwood: Maya will run the 72-hour heatmap sim and Jared will send the cost workbook. Then we'll meet next week for a deep-dive.
[59:50] Jared Kim: Perfect. I'll follow up with calendar invite and the spreadsheet. Thanks everyone.
[60:00] End of recording.
notes: Maya attached a sample CSV and quickstart deck during screen share (reference deck: /decks/optimize-playbook.pdf)
Polaris asked for KMS integration details and dedicated pool ROI comparison
